# Installation

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Install the release from CRAN:
install.packages("NACHO")

# Or install the development version as a binary package from R-universe,
# which does not need Rtools or Xcode:
install.packages(
  "NACHO",
  repos = c("https://mcanouil.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org")
)

# Or build the latest commit from GitHub with pak:
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("mcanouil/NACHO")
```

```{r}
#| message: false
# Load NACHO
library(NACHO)
```

# Load RCC files

*NACHO* ships three small datasets in `inst/extdata`, so every chunk below runs offline.
`GSE178516` holds six mRNA samples measured with the PanCancer IO 360 panel.
`GSE270837` holds six miRNA samples.
`GSE346526` holds six mRNA samples in RCC files that nSolver 4.0.1.8 wrote.
All three come from the NCBI GEO public database [@barrett_ncbi_2013], and each folder has a `samplesheet.csv` whose `IDFILE` column holds the exact name of each RCC file.

`load_rcc()` takes the folder with the RCC files, the samplesheet and the name of the identifier column.
It reads the files, computes the quality-control metrics, normalises the counts and returns a `nacho` object.
With only six samples, there are at most five principal components, so we ask for five.
The RCC files do not name the instrument, so we say it is an nCounter MAX, which sets the binding density limits.

```{r}
#| label: load
data_directory <- system.file("extdata", "GSE178516", package = "NACHO")
nacho <- load_rcc(
  data_directory = data_directory,
  ssheet_csv = file.path(data_directory, "samplesheet.csv"),
  id_colname = "IDFILE",
  instrument = "max",
  n_comp = 5
)
print(nacho)
```

# Read the object

Four accessors give you the content of a `nacho` object as plain matrices and data frames.
`nacho_counts()` returns the counts, with one row per probe and one column per sample.
Pass `normalised = TRUE` for the normalised counts, and `log2 = TRUE` for `log2(count + 1)`.

```{r}
#| label: counts
head(nacho_counts(nacho), n = c(5, 3))
```

`nacho_samples()` has one row per sample, with the samplesheet columns, the RCC header fields and the quality-control metrics.

```{r}
#| label: samples
head(nacho_samples(nacho)[, c("IDFILE", "title", "CartridgeID", "BD", "FoV")], n = 3)
```

`nacho_probes()` has one row per probe, with its code class, its detection rate and whether it is a housekeeping gene.

```{r}
#| label: probes
head(nacho_probes(nacho), n = 3)
table(nacho_probes(nacho)[["CodeClass"]])
```

`nacho_qc()` has the quality-control table, one row per sample.

```{r}
#| label: qc
head(nacho_qc(nacho)[, c("IDFILE", "BD", "FoV", "PCL", "LoD")], n = 3)
```

Earlier versions of *NACHO* kept all of this in a `$nacho` data frame.
That slot is gone, and the article "Moving from NACHO 2" on the [package website](https://m.canouil.dev/NACHO/) maps each old element to its accessor.

# Quality control

A sample is flagged when a metric falls outside its limits.
`nacho_thresholds()` builds those limits.
The default `"nsolver"` preset follows the nCounter knowledge base, and `preset = "legacy"` reproduces the limits of *NACHO* 2.

```{r}
#| label: thresholds
str(nacho_thresholds(), max.level = 1)
```

Each `*_status` column of `nacho_qc()` holds the result of one check.
Three more columns summarise them: `status`, `n_flags` and `reason`.

```{r}
#| label: flags
nacho_qc(nacho)[, c("IDFILE", "status", "n_flags", "reason")]
```

All six samples pass.
To use the legacy limits, give `load_rcc()` the preset, or pass new limits to `normalise()`.

```{r}
#| label: legacy
legacy <- load_rcc(
  data_directory = data_directory,
  ssheet_csv = file.path(data_directory, "samplesheet.csv"),
  id_colname = "IDFILE",
  instrument = "max",
  n_comp = 5,
  preset = "legacy"
)
table(nacho_qc(legacy)[["status"]])
```

`write_thresholds()` saves a set of limits to a YAML file, and `read_thresholds()` reads the file back.
With this file, you can use the same limits for each study.
The **Export** page of the app writes the same file.

```{r}
#| label: thresholds-file
thresholds_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".yml")
write_thresholds(nacho_thresholds(preset = "legacy"), thresholds_file)
legacy <- normalise(nacho, outliers_thresholds = read_thresholds(thresholds_file))
table(nacho_qc(legacy)[["status"]])
```

# Normalise

`normalise()` normalises a `nacho` object again with new settings and returns a new object.
The default scales the samples with the geometric mean of the positive controls (`"GEO"`).
`"GLM"` fits a Poisson model to the positive and negative controls instead.

```{r}
#| label: normalise
geo_norm <- normalise(nacho, normalisation_method = "GEO")
glm_norm <- normalise(nacho, normalisation_method = "GLM")
head(nacho_counts(glm_norm, normalised = TRUE), n = c(3, 3))
```

Background handling has two arguments.
`background` chooses how to estimate each sample's background from its negative controls, for example `"mean_2sd"`.
`background_mode` chooses what to do with it: `"threshold"` raises lower counts to the background, and `"subtract"` removes it.

```{r}
#| label: background
background <- normalise(
  nacho,
  background = "mean_2sd",
  background_mode = "subtract"
)
```

`exclude_outliers()` drops the flagged samples and normalises the remaining ones again.
Here nothing is flagged, so the object stays as it is.

```{r}
#| label: exclude
cleaned <- exclude_outliers(geo_norm)
```

# miRNA panels

`load_rcc()` recognises miRNA panels from their probes.
The folder `GSE270837` holds six samples from such a panel, measured on an nCounter SPRINT, so we load them with the SPRINT limits.

```{r}
#| label: mirna
mirna_directory <- system.file("extdata", "GSE270837", package = "NACHO")
mirna <- load_rcc(
  data_directory = mirna_directory,
  ssheet_csv = file.path(mirna_directory, "samplesheet.csv"),
  id_colname = "IDFILE",
  instrument = "sprint",
  n_comp = 5
)
print(mirna)
table(nacho_probes(mirna)[["CodeClass"]])
```

The housekeeping mRNAs of a miRNA panel sit at the background level, so housekeeping normalisation is off by default.
It only switches on when you pass `housekeeping_genes` or set `housekeeping_predict = TRUE`.
The miRNA methods of `normalisation_method` (`"stable_mirna"`, `"total_mirna"`, `"spike_in"` and `"ligation"`) scale the samples with miRNAs or with the spike-in and ligation controls instead.

`Ligation_NEG` flags a sample when its largest ligation negative control is above the detection limit.
Whole-blood RNA raises the ligation negative `LIG_NEG_A` together with red blood cell miRNAs such as miR-451a.
Thus most samples of a whole-blood study can fail `Ligation_NEG` without a fault in the assay.
When more than half of the samples fail, `load_rcc()` warns about this pattern.
For whole-blood samples, set a higher upper bound for `Ligation_NEG` and normalise again.
The bound below is an example; choose it from the `Ligation_NEG` values of your study.

```{r}
#| label: mirna-whole-blood
#| eval: false
thresholds <- nacho_thresholds(instrument = "sprint")
thresholds[["Ligation_NEG"]] <- c(-Inf, 100)
mirna <- normalise(mirna, outliers_thresholds = thresholds)
```

# Plots

`autoplot()` draws any quality-control figure of the app and of the report.
It takes the object and a `type`, and returns a `ggplot` object.

```{r}
#| label: plot-bd
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Box plot of the binding density of each cartridge, with the limits of
#|   the quality control drawn as dashed lines.
autoplot(nacho, type = "BD")
```

Every `type` takes the same arguments: `colour`, `size`, `show_legend`, `show_outliers`, `outliers_factor`, `outliers_labels` and `dark`.
A few plot types ignore some of them, and `?autoplot.nacho` says which.
The relative log expression of the normalised counts shows whether the samples line up.

```{r}
#| label: plot-rle
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Box plots of the relative log expression of each sample, centred on zero.
autoplot(geo_norm, type = "RLE")
```

The first two principal components show how the samples spread.

```{r}
#| label: plot-pca
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Scatter plot of the first two principal components, with one point per
#|   sample coloured by cartridge.
autoplot(geo_norm, type = "PCA12")
```

This table lists every plot type.

| `type` | What it shows |
|:---|:---|
| `"BD"` | Binding Density. |
| `"FoV"` | Field of View (imaging). |
| `"PCL"` | Positive Control Linearity. |
| `"LoD"` | Limit of Detection. |
| `"Positive"` | Positive controls. |
| `"Negative"` | Negative controls. |
| `"Housekeeping"` | Housekeeping genes. |
| `"PN"` | Positive controls against negative controls. |
| `"ACBD"` | Average counts against binding density. |
| `"ACMC"` | Average counts against median counts. |
| `"PCA12"` | Principal component 1 against 2. |
| `"PCAi"` | Scree plot of the principal components. |
| `"PCA"` | Planes of the first principal components. |
| `"PFNF"` | Positive factor against negative factor. |
| `"HF"` | Housekeeping factor. |
| `"NORM"` | Normalisation factor. |
| `"Stability"` | geNorm stability of the housekeeping genes. |
| `"RLE"` | Relative log expression of the normalised endogenous genes. |
| `"BatchFactors"` | Normalisation factors by cartridge. |
| `"PCBatch"` | Share of each principal component explained by cartridge and date. |

# Report

`render()` builds a report with every quality-control metric and a description of each.
It writes a self-contained HTML file, or a Typst PDF with `format = "typst"`, and returns the path.
It needs Quarto 1.9.18 or newer.
The article "The Quality-Control Report" on the [package website](https://m.canouil.dev/NACHO/) shows what the report looks like.

```{r}
#| label: render
#| eval: false
render(nacho, format = "html", output_dir = tempdir())
```

# App

`visualise()` opens the interactive app.
The sidebar holds the quality-control thresholds and the normalisation settings for every page.
When you click Done, `visualise()` returns the tuned object to your R session.

```{r}
#| label: app
#| eval: false
tuned <- visualise(nacho)
```

```{r}
#| label: app-fig
#| echo: false
#| out-width: 650px
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   NACHO app on the QC metrics page, with the threshold sliders on the left
#|   and box plots of binding density and field of view for each cartridge.
knitr::include_graphics(path = "README-app.png")
```

The article "Explore quality control in the app" on the [package website](https://m.canouil.dev/NACHO/) walks through every page of the app.

# Bioconductor

`as_summarized_experiment()` converts a `nacho` object into a `SummarizedExperiment`, and `as_nacho()` converts it back.
This needs the *SummarizedExperiment* package from Bioconductor.

```{r}
#| label: bioconductor
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("SummarizedExperiment", quietly = TRUE)
se <- as_summarized_experiment(nacho)
se
```
